tagline: Across Iowa on town streets the through highway left behind.
intro: Iowa’s Lincoln Highway Heritage Byway crosses farmland from the Loess Hills near the Missouri River to central plains, river valleys and the Mississippi bluffs. The route is mostly paved, with gravel loops. The Iowa DOT guide highlights historic main streets, bridges and original 1928 markers as features of this National Scenic Byway.

Established in 1913 as a memorial to Abraham Lincoln, the transcontinental highway linked Times Square with San Francisco. Its Iowa route deliberately connected downtowns to draw attention to the Good Roads Movement. US 30 took over in 1926, and later straightening bypassed towns. Straightening began in the 1930s; later, long stretches of US 30 became a four-lane expressway as traffic increased. After years of lobbying by the revived Lincoln Highway Association, Iowa designated the historic route its first Heritage Byway in 2006. The heritage route preserves a journey through those bypassed communities.

Travel east from Council Bluffs through Carroll toward Boone and Ames. South of Boone, Ledges State Park offers a sandstone gorge; at Colo, Reed-Niland Corner marks the Lincoln and Jefferson highways’ junction. Mount Vernon’s uptown and Cornell College occupy opposite ends of a wind-shaped ridge. Continue through Marshalltown and Cedar Rapids to Mount Vernon, then through the eastern towns toward Clinton.

moments.title: Ledges State Park
moments.text: Pea’s Creek cuts a sandstone gorge south of Boone, reaching 100 feet deep in places. Concretions project from its cliffs, and the park contains stone buildings and bridges constructed by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s. Water has also changed the lower park: repeated flooding associated with Saylorville Lake has reduced timbered areas and left silt behind. A pole in the lowlands records past flood levels. Even the largest recorded floods cover only a small portion of the park. A winding, single-lane canyon road crosses Pea’s and Davis creeks at five points, beneath sandstone walls and bluffs.

moments.title: Reed-Niland Corner, Colo
moments.text: Gas, food and a bed came together at the crossing of the Lincoln and Jefferson highways in Colo. Farmer Charlie Reed began with a gas station in 1923, then added cabins for travelers. A lunch stand became a cafe in 1926 with help from his nephew C. Reed Niland. During the 1920s and early 1930s, the cafe and station were among the Lincoln Highway’s few round-the-clock stops. The cafe and gas station moved to their present positions within the complex in 1930. A motel replaced the cabins in 1947; Reed’s gas station now serves as a museum.

moments.title: Mount Vernon
moments.text: Mount Vernon’s “mountain” is a paha: a ridge of sand and loess formed along the prevailing wind during the ice ages. The ridge runs roughly one mile along a roughly northwest-to-southeast axis. It rises up to 100 feet above the surrounding country, with uptown at its southeast end and Cornell College to the northwest. Travelers stopped here before the Lincoln Highway existed. By 1838, the settlement was known as Pinhook, a stop on the Military Road between Dubuque and Iowa City. It took the name Mount Vernon in 1847, honoring George Washington’s estate.
